title: A First Win32 Application
summary: Put the last lesson together into a complete windowed program: `wWinMain`, registering a class, creating a window, a game-style loop, and drawing a moving square with GDI using a back buffer so it does not flicker. About 120 lines of plain Windows API, and every one explained.
ideas:
- Build and run the program. Resize the window and check the square bounces off the new edges.
- Make the arrow keys change the square's velocity by handling more `WM_KEYDOWN` codes (`VK_LEFT`, `VK_RIGHT`, ...).
- Remove `DeleteObject(teal);`, run the program, and watch its GDI object count in Task Manager's Details tab.
- Remove the back buffer and draw directly to `screen`. Can you see the flicker?

cards.q: What are the main steps of a Win32 program's start-up?
cards.a:
Register a window class with a window procedure, create a window of that class, show it, then run the message loop

A window can only be created from a class that has already been registered.

cards.q: What is the client area of a window?
cards.a:
The part inside the borders and title bar, where the program draws

That is why `AdjustWindowRect` is used: to make the client area the size you want, the whole window must be a little larger.

cards.q: What must you do with every GDI object you create?
cards.a:
Delete it when finished, after deselecting it from any device context it was selected into

GDI objects are a limited resource; leaking them every frame eventually stops drawing working.

cards.q: Why does the program call `AdjustWindowRect` before `CreateWindowExW`?
cards.a:
The size includes borders, so it must grow to fit the client area

The client area is the drawable part inside the frame.

cards.q: What does drawing into an off-screen bitmap and copying it with `BitBlt` prevent?
cards.a:
Flicker: no half-drawn frame is ever shown

This technique is called double buffering.

cards.q: Why does the square move by `velocity * dt`?
cards.a:
So its speed is the same at any frame rate

A fixed step per frame would make it faster on faster computers.
